exercises.title: Welcome to Chapter 4
exercises.body: Reading is one direction — now you write. Below every exercise sits the Shavian keyboard, laid out like the alphabet chart you learned from: each deep letter directly under its tall partner, each long vowel under its short one. Hunt by sound family and you’ll find any letter fast. It shows only the keys an answer needs, so it starts as bare letters and grows as the words do. (Real phone and computer layouts exist too — Shaw JAFL and Shaw QWERTY — for when you graduate.)

exercises.title: Spell the sound, not the letters
exercises.body: You have just spelled “cat” three ways, with less help each time — that is the shape of this whole chapter. Now forget English spelling entirely. Say the word out loud, then write one Shavian letter per sound you hear. “Fish” is three sounds — f, i, sh — so it is three letters: 𐑓 𐑦 𐑖.

exercises.title: Longer words, same rule
exercises.body: Nothing changes as the words grow — you still write one letter per sound you hear, left to right. Milk is four sounds and four letters, 𐑥𐑦𐑤𐑒. Hand is four, 𐑣𐑨𐑯𐑛. Say the word under your breath and let your hand follow your mouth.

exercises.title: Names need the dot
exercises.body: Remember the naming dot? When you write a name it goes first — and since the next answer is a name, a · key appears with it, below the letters.

exercises.title: A start
exercises.body: That’s your first Shavian written by hand — well, by keyboard. The rest of the chapter builds on it: hearing vowels correctly, the r-vowels, the little words, the endings, the schwa, then the two things English makes hard and Shavian makes easy — apostrophes and its/it’s — and finally whole sentences. For now, enjoy having written the alphabet you spent three chapters learning to read.
